passages.title: The Lost Key
sentences: Ben and Ana got off the bus after school.
Ben looked in his bag for the house key.
The key was gone.
Ben frowned and looked in every pocket.
Ana went back to the bus stop.
She looked under the bench.
Then she held up a shiny key.
Ben grinned.
"Thank you!" he said.

passages.title: The Rover Ramp
sentences: Priya brought her rover to the robot fair at Harbor Middle School.
Her job was to drive it up a steep wooden ramp.
The rover rolled halfway up and then stopped.
Its battery was empty.
Priya groaned and put her hands on her head.
She had worked on the rover for three weeks.
She found a charger and plugged the rover in.
While she waited, she checked every wire.
Twenty minutes later, she tried again.
This time the rover climbed all the way to the top.
Priya smiled at Ms. Ortiz.
She had fixed it all by herself.

passages.title: The Milkmaid and Her Pail
sentences: A farm girl walked to market with a pail of milk on her head.
As she walked, she made plans.
"I will sell this milk and buy some eggs," she thought.
"The eggs will hatch into chickens."
"I will sell the chickens and buy a new blue dress."
She smiled and gave a happy little skip.
She pictured the dress and tossed her head with pride.
The pail tipped over.
All the milk spilled onto the dusty road.
The girl looked at the empty pail.
Her eggs, her chickens and her new dress were all gone.
Tears came to her eyes.

credit.title: The Milkmaid and Her Pail
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Maya's Comic
sentences: The library put up a comic show, and Maya's comic was on the wall.
It was about a rock that rolled all the way down Lantern Peaks.
On the first day of the show, Maya stood at the back of the room.
Her hands felt cold, and her stomach felt tight.
This was the first time strangers would see her drawings.
What if they thought her comic was boring?
A boy of about eight stopped in front of it.
He read every box, and then he laughed out loud at the last one.
"The rock does a flip into the creek!" he told his dad.
Then he turned around and saw Maya's name tag.
"Did you draw that?" he asked. "Can you sign my map of the show?"
Maya signed her name in big letters.
She smiled the whole way home.
That night, she drew three new comics.

passages.title: The Old Oak
sentences: For many years, a giant oak tree stood in the middle of Harbor Park.
Sam and his friends met under it after school.
Pixel liked to nap in its shade.
But the tree was very old, and its trunk was soft and weak inside.
Workers from the town said it had to come down.
On Monday, workers cut the tree down.
Sam stood by the fence and looked at the empty spot.
His eyes filled with tears.
He would miss the shade and the bumpy roots where he sat.
On Saturday, Grandma Rose came to the park with a small oak in a pot.
Sam, Priya and Leo dug a hole and planted it in the same spot.
Sam patted the soil flat.
"One day, this tree will be big too," he said, and he smiled.

passages.title: Ben's Game Song
sentences: In music class, each student had to make a short song on the school computer.
Ben and Ana had already built a racing game together, so Ben decided to make music for it.
His first song was slow and soft.
When Ana played the game with his song, she yawned, and her car drifted off the track.
Ben slumped down in his chair and stared at the screen.
Then he had an idea.
He made the beat twice as fast and added loud drums.
This time, Ana leaned forward and gripped the controller tightly.
"This music makes me want to go faster!" she said, and she won the race.
On Friday, the music teacher played Ben's song for the whole class.
Three students asked if they could play the game, too.
Ben grinned and saved his song in a folder called Best Work.

passages.title: Kite Day
sentences: On Saturday, Priya and Maya carried a big red kite up to the lookout on Lantern Peaks.
They had spent two evenings building it from thin sticks, paper and string.
But when they reached the top, the air was completely still.
The kite just dragged through the grass behind them.
Maya sat down on a rock and sighed.
Priya checked the weather forecast on her phone.
"It says the wind will get stronger in the afternoon," she said.
So they ate their lunch on the rock and watched the clouds.
At two o'clock, the tall grass began to bend, and Maya's hair blew across her face.
Priya let out the string, and the kite rose higher and higher over the trees.
Maya laughed and clapped her hands.
Later, a line of gray clouds moved in from the sea, and the wind turned cold.
The girls wound up the string and walked down before the first drops of rain.
Maya was not upset, because the kite had flown higher than they had hoped.

passages.title: The Lark and Her Young Ones
sentences: A mother lark built her nest on the ground in the middle of a farmer's wheat field.
Her chicks hatched in spring and grew strong while the green wheat grew tall around them.
By summer, the wheat had turned golden, and the young larks were almost ready to fly.
One morning, while their mother was away finding food, the farmer and his son walked into the field.
"This wheat is ripe," said the farmer. "We must ask our neighbors to come and help us cut it."
The young larks huddled together in the nest, very worried.
When their mother returned, they all chirped at once and begged her to move them somewhere safe.
"Did the farmer say he would cut the wheat himself?" she asked.
"No, he will ask his neighbors to help," they answered.
"Then there is no need to worry yet," said the mother lark, and she calmly fed them their supper.
The neighbors were busy harvesting their own fields, so nobody came.
A few days later, the farmer returned and said, "Tomorrow we will ask our cousins to help us."
Once again, the young larks were upset, but their mother stayed calm.
"Cousins have their own work to do," she said. "We can stay here a little longer."
On his third visit, the farmer looked at the ripe wheat and shook his head.
"We cannot wait for anyone else," he told his son. "At sunrise tomorrow, you and I will cut this field ourselves."
When the mother lark heard this, she gathered her young ones at once.
"Now it is time to leave," she said. "When a farmer decides to do the work himself, it will certainly get done."
That evening, the whole family flew to a new home beside the forest.

credit.title: The Lark and Her Young Ones
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Harbor Fun Run
sentences: Every June, Harbor Town holds a five-kilometer fun run along the harbor path.
This year, Leo wanted to finish in under thirty minutes, so he had trained three mornings a week since March.
Maya was entering the race for the first time.
She had never run farther than two kilometers before, and her only goal was to finish without stopping.
Leo started fast and passed many runners in the first kilometer.
By the fourth kilometer, his legs felt heavy, and he had to slow down.
He crossed the finish line, looked up at the big clock and saw thirty-one minutes.
Leo put his hands on his knees and stared at the ground.
He had missed his goal by one minute.
A few minutes later, Ana, who was helping at the finish table, came over with a list of last year's times.
"Look," she said, pointing at his name. "Last year you finished in thirty-four minutes."
Leo read the list twice.
He had run three whole minutes faster than last year.
He stood up straight, and a slow smile spread across his face.
Just then, Maya came around the last corner, running slowly but steadily.
When she crossed the line, she threw both arms in the air and shouted, "I didn't stop once!"
Her time was forty-two minutes, but she did not even glance at the clock.
Leo and Ana cheered for her, and Leo suggested that next year they could all train together.

passages.title: The Day the Sun Went Dark
sentences: Last spring, my family drove for six hours to stand in the path of a total solar eclipse.
During a total eclipse, the Moon passes exactly between Earth and the Sun and covers the Sun completely.
This can only be seen from a narrow strip of land, and any one place may wait hundreds of years between total eclipses.
I had been reading about it for months, and I wanted to see it more than anything.
On the morning of the eclipse, I woke up early and looked out of our motel window.
Thick gray clouds covered the whole sky.
My stomach felt tight, and I could hardly eat any breakfast.
My dad studied the weather map on his phone, and we drove another hour west to a field where the forecast showed clear sky.
By noon, the clouds behind us had thinned, and the sky above the field was bright blue.
I let out a long breath, and my shoulders finally relaxed.
We put on special eclipse glasses, because looking straight at the Sun without them can damage your eyes.
Through the dark lenses, I watched the Moon slowly cover more and more of the Sun.
As the last sliver of sunlight disappeared, the air grew cool, and the birds in the trees went quiet.
The sky turned a deep blue, almost like night, and a few bright stars appeared.
Only during those few minutes, while the Sun was completely covered, was it safe to take our glasses off.
Where the Sun had been, there was a black circle with soft white light streaming out around it.
Everyone in the field cheered, and then they went completely silent.
I stared at it the whole time, and I forgot to take a single photo.
After about three minutes, a bright flash of sunlight burst from one edge, and we quickly put our glasses back on.
On the long drive home, I kept thinking about how tiny our field had looked under that strange, dark sky.
I have already marked the next total eclipse I can travel to on my calendar.

credit.title: The Day the Sun Went Dark
credit.author: Learning to Fly (AI-drafted)

passages.title: The Whale Watch
sentences: Every summer, small boats carry visitors out from the coast to watch humpback whales feed.
Humpbacks can grow as long as a city bus, and like all whales, they must come to the surface to breathe air.
On one trip last July, a girl of about eleven stood at the front of the boat with binoculars around her neck.
She had read three books about whales, and she knew how to spot the tall puff of mist that a whale blows out when it breathes.
For the first hour, the sea was empty.
The boat rocked from side to side, the wind was cold, and several passengers went inside to sit down.
The girl kept scanning the water, but her shoulders slowly drooped.
"Whales are wild animals, so we can never promise to see one," the captain said over the speaker.
The girl sat down on a bench and put her binoculars away.
Then, far off to the left, a puff of mist shot up from the waves.
The girl jumped to her feet and pointed, shouting, "There! A blow!"
The captain steered closer slowly and turned off the engine, so the noise would not disturb the whale.
A dark, shiny back rolled through the water, and then a huge tail rose high into the air and slid under the sea.
The underside of the tail was black and white, with a pattern of spots and scratches.
The captain explained that every humpback has its own tail pattern, so scientists can use photos to tell the whales apart.
The girl had taken a photo of the tail just before it disappeared.
The captain told her that she could send it to scientists who keep a record of every humpback tail they have seen.
On the ride back to shore, she did not seem to notice the cold wind at all.
She looked at her photo again and again, smiling at the spots on the tail.

passages.title: Pixel Rings the Bell
sentences: Sam hung a small bell on the back door.
He wanted Pixel to ring it when he needed to go outside.
Every day, Sam showed Pixel the bell and gave him a treat.
For five days, Pixel just sniffed the bell and wagged his tail.
Sam sighed, but he kept trying.
On Saturday morning, Sam was eating breakfast at the table.
Then he heard a sound from the back door.
Ding, ding!
Pixel was sitting by the door, and the bell was still swinging.
Sam jumped up and opened the door.
"You did it, Pixel!" he shouted.
Then he called Grandma Rose to tell her the news.

passages.title: The Boy and the Filberts
sentences: A boy saw a tall jar of filberts on a high shelf.
Filberts are small, round nuts, and he loved them.
He pushed his hand in and grabbed as many as he could.
Then he tried to pull his hand out.
It would not come out!
The top of the jar was too narrow for his full fist.
He did not want to drop a single nut.
He pulled and pulled, and then he began to cry.
His mother came into the kitchen.
"Hold only half as many," she said. "You can take more later."
The boy let go of some nuts, and his hand slid out easily.
He smiled and ate the nuts one at a time.

credit.title: The Boy and the Filberts
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Level Nine
sentences: Ben was stuck on level nine of his puzzle game.
He had to push ten blocks onto ten gold squares.
Every time, one block got trapped in a corner.
He tried for a whole week.
On Friday, he put down the controller and groaned.
Ana sat next to him and watched him play.
"Try moving the corner block first," she said.
Ben tried her idea.
This time, no block got trapped.
The last block slid onto the last gold square.
The screen flashed LEVEL COMPLETE.
Ben jumped off the couch and gave Ana a high five.

passages.title: The Heron
sentences: Early one morning, a tall heron walked slowly along the edge of a clear stream.
He was looking for breakfast, and the water was full of fish.
A small fish swam close to his long legs.
"That fish is far too small for a fine bird like me," said the heron, and he lifted his beak high.
Next, a young perch swam by.
"I will not open my beak for such a skinny fish," he said.
He decided to wait for a big, fat fish instead.
As the sun climbed higher, the fish swam away into the deep, cool middle of the stream.
The heron waited and waited, but no more fish came near the edge.
By noon, he was very hungry.
At last, he found a tiny snail on a rock, and he gobbled it up.
Then he thought about all the fish he had turned away.
He wished he had not been so picky.

credit.title: The Heron
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Station in the Sky
sentences: Priya's phone app said the space station would fly over Harbor Town at 7:42 that evening.
The space station is a huge science lab that circles Earth about every ninety minutes.
Astronauts live and work inside it.
Priya and her mom went out to the back yard at 7:30 and looked at the western sky.
Priya kept checking the time on her phone.
She bounced on her toes and could not stand still.
At 7:42, a bright white dot rose above the trees.
It did not blink like an airplane, and it moved smoothly across the sky.
"It shines because sunlight bounces off it," said her mom.
Priya watched without saying a word.
Somewhere inside that tiny dot, real people were eating supper or looking down at Earth.
After about five minutes, the dot faded and disappeared.
Priya let out a long breath.
"Can we watch it again next week?" she asked.

passages.title: The Penalty Kick
sentences: Ana and Ben's soccer team was tied 1 to 1, and only two minutes were left in the game.
Then a defender bumped into Ben inside the penalty area, and the referee blew a whistle.
Their team would get a penalty kick.
"Who wants to take it?" asked Coach Novak.
Nobody answered.
Ana's heart was pounding, but she raised her hand.
She had practiced penalty kicks every day after school for a month.
She set the ball on the white spot and chose the left corner of the goal.
She took three steps back and breathed out slowly.
Then she ran forward and kicked.
The ball flew past the goalkeeper's fingers and into the net.
Her teammates ran over and cheered, and Ben gave her a huge hug.
Ana could not stop smiling all the way home.

passages.title: Blue Sparks
sentences: On a warm summer night, Grandma Rose took Sam and Leo down to the beach after dark.
She had heard that the waves were glowing.
At first, Leo laughed and said it was probably just the moon.
Then a small wave broke on the sand, and a line of bright blue light ran along its edge.
Leo stopped laughing and stared.
Grandma Rose explained that the sea was full of tiny living things called plankton.
Some kinds of plankton make a flash of blue light when the water around them moves.
Sam waded into the shallow water up to his ankles.
Every time he kicked, blue sparks swirled around his feet.
Leo ran in next to him and pulled his hand through the water, making long blue streaks.
"It looks like a video game!" Leo whispered.
The boys stayed until Grandma Rose said it was time to go home.
On the walk back, Sam asked her if the plankton would glow again tomorrow night.

passages.title: The Lumpy Rolls
sentences: On Saturday, Grandma Rose let Sam make the dinner rolls at her bakery.
He mixed the flour, water, yeast and salt, just like she showed him.
Then he shaped the dough into twelve rolls.
Grandma Rose's rolls were always perfectly round.
Sam's rolls came out of the oven lumpy and uneven, and one looked like a potato.
Sam's face turned red, and he pushed the tray to the back of the counter.
"Nobody will want these," he said quietly.
Just then, Mrs. Lin from the Lighthouse Café came in to buy bread.
She saw the tray and asked if she could try one.
She took a bite and closed her eyes.
"These are soft and warm inside," she said. "I will take all twelve for my café."
Sam looked at Grandma Rose, and she nodded and smiled.
That afternoon, Sam walked past the café and saw his rolls in the window with a sign that said FRESH TODAY.

passages.title: The Donkey and the Load of Salt
sentences: A merchant sold salt in a market town on the far side of a river.
Every week, he loaded heavy sacks of salt onto his donkey's back, and the two of them walked to market together.
On the way, they had to cross the river at a shallow place called a ford.
One morning, the donkey slipped on a smooth stone in the ford and fell into the water.
When he struggled back to his feet, the load on his back felt much lighter.
Much of the salt had melted away in the river.
The donkey trotted the rest of the way to market, feeling very pleased with himself.
The merchant was not pleased at all, because he had lost half of the salt he planned to sell.
On the next trip, the donkey remembered what had happened.
At the ford, he lay down in the water on purpose, and once again his load became light.
The merchant frowned as they walked on, and he began to think.
He guessed that the second fall had not been an accident.
The following week, the merchant filled the donkey's sacks with sponges instead of salt.
The sponges were light and dry, and the donkey felt sure that his trick would work again.
At the ford, he lay down in the river and waited.
But sponges do not melt the way salt does, because they soak up water instead.
When the donkey stood up, his load was far heavier than before, and he had to stagger slowly all the way home.
He never lay down in the river again.

credit.title: The Donkey and the Load of Salt
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: A Raven and a Swan
sentences: A raven lived at the edge of a farm, where he found plenty of food in the fields every day.
His feathers were black from the top of his head to the tip of his tail.
One morning, he saw a swan gliding across the pond near the farmhouse.
Her feathers were so white that they shone in the sun.
The raven watched her for a long time, and he began to feel jealous.
"If I lived in the water like the swan, my feathers would turn white too," he told himself.
So the raven left the fields, where he always found food, and moved to the edge of the pond.
Every day, he splashed in the water and scrubbed his feathers with his beak.
He washed in the morning, at noon and again before the sun went down.
But his feathers stayed exactly as black as before.
The pond had none of the seeds and insects that he liked to eat, so he grew hungry and tired.
At last, the raven stood on the bank and looked at his reflection in the water.
He was still black, and now he was thin as well.
Slowly, he understood that washing could not change the color he was born with.
He flew back to the fields and ate until he was full.
From then on, he let the swan be white, and he was glad to be a raven.

credit.title: A Raven and a Swan
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Trail Map
sentences: In May, Harbor Town opened a new bike trail through Story Woods.
It curved past the old mill, crossed the creek on a wooden bridge and ended at the campsite.
Every day, riders came into Okafor's Bike Shop to ask how to find it, and Mr. Okafor explained the route again and again.
Some days, he answered the same question twenty times while a row of broken bikes waited for repairs.
Sam had an idea.
On Saturday, he rode the whole trail with a notebook and a small meter on his handlebars that measured distance.
At every turn, he stopped and wrote down how far he had come.
That week, he spent four evenings drawing a map at the kitchen table.
He marked the bridge, the mill and the steep hill, and he added a scale bar so riders could measure distances.
Mr. Okafor printed one hundred copies and put them in a box by the door with a sign that said FREE TRAIL MAPS.
The next Saturday, a family of four came back to the shop, muddy and smiling.
The father held up Sam's map and said it was the only reason they had found the campsite.
Sam's ears turned pink, and he looked down at his shoes, but he was grinning.
Mr. Okafor laughed and pointed to his work bench.
"Thanks to you, I fixed six bikes today instead of two," he said.
By the end of June, the box of maps was empty, and Mr. Okafor asked Sam to draw a second trail map.

passages.title: The Ore Cart
sentences: On the first Saturday in May, Mr. Varga's rock club visited the Ridgeway Mine Museum, where he also works as a guide.
Maya had joined the club because she loved minerals, and she brought Sam along because the museum had old mine carts on rails.
Long ago, miners pushed these carts through the tunnels to carry rock out of the hill.
Sam had read that visitors could ride a cart along a short track outside the museum, and he had talked about it all week.
When they arrived, a sign beside the track said CLOSED FOR REPAIRS.
Sam stopped walking and read the sign twice.
His shoulders dropped, and he hardly said a word during the tour of the first tunnel.
Maya felt the opposite.
Mr. Varga let the club search a pile of waste rock that the miners had left behind, and each member could keep one piece.
Within ten minutes, Maya found a lump of rock streaked with bright green malachite, a mineral that forms where there is copper.
She held it up to the light and grinned.
After the search, Mr. Varga noticed Sam standing alone by the closed track.
He explained that one rail had cracked, and a worker was coming to replace it next week.
Then he led Sam into a shed and showed him the museum's oldest cart, which had iron wheels and a box that tipped forward to dump out the rock.
Mr. Varga even let Sam push the cart a few meters along the rails inside the shed.
On the bus ride home, Maya turned her malachite over and over in her hands, and Sam told everyone exactly how the cart's box tipped forward.

passages.title: The Broken String
sentences: Sam had been learning the guitar in the school music club since September.
In March, Ms. Gray invited him to play one song by himself at the library's Music Afternoon.
He practiced the song every evening for three weeks, until he could play it without looking at his fingers.
Even so, he had never performed alone in front of strangers, and just imagining it made his hands feel cold.
Twenty minutes before the show, Sam sat in a back room to warm up.
As he tightened one of the thin strings, it snapped with a sharp twang.
Sam stared at the loose string, and his face felt hot.
He had no spare strings in his guitar case.
Ms. Gray looked in her bag and found a new pack of guitar strings.
She helped him put the new string on, and together they tuned it.
She warned him that new strings stretch and can slip out of tune, and she told him to continue playing if that happened.
When Sam's name was called, he walked to the chair at the front of the room.
Grandma Rose was sitting in the second row, and she gave him a small wave.
Sam checked the new string one more time, took a deep breath and began.
Halfway through, the new string sounded slightly too low, but he continued playing, exactly as Ms. Gray had advised.
When he finished, the audience applauded loudly, and a small girl in the front row asked if he could play it again.
Sam laughed, and his hands did not feel cold anymore.

passages.title: The Climbing Wall
sentences: For Leo's birthday, his dad took Leo, Maya and Ana to the climbing gym near the harbor.
Every climber wore a harness clipped to a rope, and a worker on the ground held the other end of the rope.
The tallest wall was ten meters high, and it was covered with colored holds shaped like small rocks.
Leo had climbed many times before, and he raced to the top of the easiest route in less than a minute.
He rang the bell at the top, came back down and shrugged.
"That was too easy," he said.
Maya had never climbed before.
On her first try, she stopped halfway up, holding on tightly and looking down at the floor.
The worker told her she could come down whenever she liked, so she did.
On her second try, she reached a little higher, but her arms got tired.
Ana showed her how to push up with her legs instead of pulling with her arms.
On her third try, Maya moved slowly and used her legs the way Ana had shown her.
When she reached the top, she rang the bell so hard that everyone in the gym looked up.
Back on the ground, her legs were shaking, but she was smiling so widely that her cheeks hurt.
Leo looked at her for a moment.
Then he walked over to the hardest route on the wall, a line of tiny purple holds, and said, "Okay, my turn to try something hard."

passages.title: The Fossil Lab Window
sentences: Last winter, my class visited a natural history museum that has a fossil lab with a large glass window.
Through the window, visitors can watch scientists called preparators remove rock from around dinosaur bones.
Fossils arrive at the lab wrapped in hard jackets of plaster, which protect them on the long trip from the dig site.
Before the trip, I had imagined an exciting room full of people uncovering giant skeletons.
Instead, I saw one woman sitting very still at a table, bent over a gray lump of rock.
She held a tool shaped like a thick pen, and it buzzed quietly as she pressed its tip against the rock.
A sign explained that the tool is called an air scribe, and it works like a tiny jackhammer, chipping away a few grains of rock at a time.
I watched for ten minutes, and I could not see anything change at all.
Most of my classmates had already wandered off to the gift shop, and I was about to follow them.
Then the preparator noticed me and waved me over to a small speaker in the wall beside the window.
She explained that she had been working on this one block of rock for three months.
She turned her magnifying lamp so I could see the spot she was uncovering, and I noticed a smooth, dark, curved shape poking out of the gray rock.
"That is the tip of a claw," she said. "You are the first person besides me to see it in about seventy-five million years."
I pressed my hands against the glass and could not stop staring.
Before I left, I asked her how she could stay patient doing such slow work every day.
She smiled and said that every grain she removed brought her a little closer to something nobody had ever seen.
On the bus back to school, my classmates showed off the plastic dinosaurs they had bought, but I kept thinking about the claw.
I have already asked whether the museum lets students volunteer in the lab when they are older.

passages.title: The Mountain Railway
sentences: Last summer, my grandfather took me on a mountain railway that climbs slopes far steeper than ordinary trains can handle.
An ordinary train has smooth metal wheels on smooth rails, so on a very steep hill its wheels would slip.
This railway has a third rail in the middle of the track, and the top of that rail is lined with metal teeth.
Under the train, a gear wheel fits into the teeth, so the train can pull itself up the mountain one tooth at a time without sliding back.
My grandfather had ridden this railway once before, when he was nine years old, with his own father.
While we waited on the platform, he told me he still remembered the smell of the engine and the cold wind at the top.
Then he stood quietly, holding the ticket from his first trip, which he had kept for sixty years.
About halfway up, the track tilted so steeply that my water bottle rolled to the back of the car.
Through the side window, the valley floor seemed to drop away beneath us, and I gripped the edge of my seat with both hands.
My grandfather noticed and pointed at the floor of the car, where we could hear a steady clicking sound.
"That is the gear catching each tooth," he said. "As long as you hear that, it is holding us safely."
I listened to the clicking, and slowly my hands relaxed.
At the summit, the air was so cold that we could see our breath, even though it was July.
I ran from one side of the viewing platform to the other, pointing out lakes and villages I had only seen on a map.
My grandfather stood at the railing for a long time without speaking.
When he turned around, his eyes were shiny, and he said he was happy that the view was exactly as he remembered it.
Then he handed me his old ticket and told me to keep it for the next sixty years.

passages.title: Robot Day at the Library
sentences: Every spring, the Harbor Town Library holds Robot Day, when older students show their inventions to younger children.
This year, Priya brought her rover, which she had rebuilt as a drawing robot.
She had attached a marker to its back so the tip touched the floor, and she had programmed the rover to draw shapes on a large sheet of paper.
A child could type a shape into her tablet, such as a square or a star, and the rover would drive along the lines and draw it.
Priya had tested it on her bedroom carpet more than twenty times, and every shape had come out neat and straight.
At the library, Mrs. Hall spread a sheet of shiny paper across the smooth floor of the meeting room.
A boy of about six typed STAR and pressed GO.

Priya felt her face grow warm, because a crowd of parents was watching.
But the boy clapped and shouted, "It made a star flower!"
He asked if he could take the drawing home, and two other children lined up to make star flowers of their own.

At home, the carpet had gripped the wheels, but on the shiny paper they spun without pushing the rover forward.
She borrowed four rubber bands from Mrs. Hall's desk and stretched one around each wheel so they would grip better.
On the next try, the rover drew a perfect square, and the parents clapped.
By the end of the afternoon, Priya's rover had drawn more than thirty shapes.

On the walk home, she thought it was strange that her favorite moment of the day had begun with a mistake.

passages.title: The Game Showcase
sentences: For six weeks, Ana and Leo built a video game together in the after-school coding club at Harbor Middle School.
In their game, a small robot named Bolt rolls through a city to deliver packages.
Ana designed the levels, and she spent most of her time on the last one, a maze of moving platforms that she had rebuilt seven times.
Leo wrote everything the characters said, and he filled the game with jokes, such as a grumpy mailbox that complained about getting too many letters.
At the end of the term, the club held a showcase, and anyone could come to the school gym to play the students' games.
For the first hour, Leo could hardly stop smiling.
Players laughed out loud at the grumpy mailbox, and one girl read every joke aloud to her little brother.
Ana, however, was watching the screen, not the players' faces.
Every player who reached the last level fell off the moving platforms within a minute, and most of them gave up and went to try another game.
After the fifth player walked away, Ana crossed her arms and stopped talking.
She wondered whether all her hard work on the maze had been a mistake.
Near the end of the showcase, a tall boy sat down and played the whole game without saying a word.
When he reached the maze, he fell off again and again, but each time he tried a different path.
On his twelfth try, he jumped onto the final platform and guided the robot safely to the last mailbox.
He threw both arms in the air and cheered so loudly that half the gym turned around.
Then he turned to Ana and asked whether she had designed the maze.
When she nodded, he said it was the best level he had played all day, because it made him think.
Ana uncrossed her arms, and for the rest of the afternoon she stood beside the screen, giving small hints to anyone who got stuck.
On the way out, Leo told her that people had laughed at his jokes, but her level was the part they would remember.

passages.title: The Weather Balloon
sentences: Every day, at hundreds of places around the world, weather scientists release large balloons filled with a light gas, such as helium.
Each balloon carries a small box of instruments that measures the temperature, the air pressure and the moisture in the air as it rises.
As the balloon climbs, the air around it gets thinner, so the balloon slowly swells until it bursts, often more than thirty kilometers above the ground.
Then the box floats back down on a small parachute.
In April, Ms. Ortiz's science class launched a weather balloon of its own from the field behind Harbor Middle School.
Priya had spent three weeks building the instrument box, which held a thermometer, a battery and a tracker that sent out its location every minute.
Sam had volunteered to follow the tracker on a map on the classroom computer.
At ten o'clock, the class counted down, and the white balloon rose quickly into the clear sky until it was only a dot.
For the next hour, Sam did not leave the screen.
He traced the balloon's path with his finger as the wind carried it east across the bay, and he called out its height every few minutes.
Priya stood behind him with her arms folded tightly.
The map showed the wind pushing the balloon toward the open sea, and if the box landed in the water, it would be lost along with all its measurements.
At 11:20, the height suddenly began to drop, which meant the balloon had burst.
The dot drifted lower and lower over the bay, and Priya held her breath.
At 11:58, the dot stopped moving.
Sam zoomed in on the map and laughed.
The box had landed in a cabbage field on Gull Island, only two hundred meters from the shore.
Priya let out her breath and sat down on the nearest chair.
That afternoon, Ms. Ortiz, Priya and Sam took the ferry across the bay, and the farmer met them at his gate with the box in his hands.
Back in class, Priya connected the box to the computer and found that the temperature high above them had dropped to fifty-five degrees Celsius below zero.
Sam printed the balloon's path and pinned it to the wall, and Priya stood in front of it for a long time.

sentences: Leo's bike chain had been slipping for a week, but he kept riding to school anyway, because he did not want to admit that he needed help.
On Wednesday afternoon, the chain fell off completely in front of Okafor's Bike Shop, and Leo stood on the sidewalk, staring at his greasy hands.
Mr. Okafor came out of the shop, wiping his hands on a rag, and examined the chain.
Instead of repairing it himself, he handed Leo a pair of work gloves and said, "I'll explain each step, and you do the work."
He described how the chain fits over the teeth of the rear gear, and how a loose chain can be tightened by sliding the back wheel slightly backward in its frame.
Leo's first attempt was crooked, and the chain popped off again as soon as he turned the pedals.
Mr. Okafor simply nodded and said, "Again."
On the third try, the chain sat straight.
The pedals turned smoothly.
Leo rode a slow circle around the parking lot, then a faster one, listening for any clicking sound.
He returned and asked whether the shop ever needed an extra helper on Saturdays.
Mr. Okafor laughed and said that a person who could repair his own chain had made a good start.

The balloon might burst before it went very high.
Sam might lose the balloon's path on the map.
The farmer on Gull Island might keep her box.
items.hint: Read the sentence right after Priya folds her arms. What did the map show?
items.explain: Priya was worried because the wind was pushing the balloon toward the open sea. If her box landed in the water, it would be lost with all its measurements. The balloon was supposed to burst.

items.prompt: Sam and Priya watched the same screen but felt differently. Which reason best explains why Sam was excited instead of worried?
options: He was following the path on a map, and he had not spent three weeks building the box.
He already knew the box would land on Gull Island.
Ms. Ortiz had told him the box could float.
He was hoping to ride the ferry that afternoon.
items.hint: Compare each person's job in the second paragraph. Whose work could be lost in the sea?
items.explain: Sam's job was to follow the tracker on the map, and he enjoyed tracing the path. Priya had built the box over three weeks, so she had more to lose. Nobody knew where the box would land until 11:58.

items.prompt: At the end, Priya stood in front of the map for a long time. Why do you think she did that? Build your answer.
items.frame: Priya felt {0} because {1}. In the story, {2}. {3}

slots.label: Feeling
options: proud
relieved
amazed
thankful

slots.label: Reason
options: her box came back safely
her box measured the air high above Earth
her three weeks of work were not lost

slots.label: Clue from the story
options: the temperature high above had dropped to fifty-five degrees Celsius below zero
the box landed only two hundred meters from the shore
the farmer met them with the box

slots.label: About me (you can skip this)
options: I would want to launch another balloon.
I would feel proud of the box too.
I would want to look at that map too.

items.hint: Read the last paragraph. Think about how Priya felt during the flight, and what happened to her box after it landed.
items.explain: One good answer is: Priya felt proud because her box measured the air high above Earth. In the story, the temperature high above had dropped to fifty-five degrees Celsius below zero. Any honest answer is fine.

items.prompt: Why did Sam grin the whole time?
options: His bridge held up after all his hard work.
Grandma Rose gave him a new train.
The bridge was easy to make.
items.hint: Read how long the bridge took. Then read what happened when the train went across.
items.explain: Sam grinned because his bridge held up after four afternoons of work. It did not bend or crack.

reason.clue: The bridge did not bend or crack.
reason.know: Seeing hard work succeed makes people want to show it off.
reason.so: So Sam grinned because his work paid off.

items.prompt: Why did Sam call Grandma Rose into the room?
options: He wanted her to see what he made.
He needed help with the glue.
The train was broken.
items.hint: Read what Sam said to Grandma Rose and what he did next.
items.explain: Sam wanted Grandma Rose to see his bridge. He said "Watch this" and sent the train across again.

items.prompt: Why did Maya feel lonely at the start of lunch?
options: Her friend was away, and everyone else sat in groups.
She did not like her sandwich.
Leo laughed at her drawing.
The lunchroom was too quiet.
items.hint: Read who was missing. Then read what everyone else in the lunchroom was doing.
items.explain: Maya felt lonely because Priya was at the dentist and everyone else was talking in groups. She ate slowly by herself.

reason.clue: Everyone seemed to be talking and laughing in groups.
reason.know: Sitting alone while others are in groups can feel lonely.
reason.so: So Maya felt lonely without Priya there.

items.prompt: Why did Maya feel better by the end of lunch?
options: Leo made room for her and showed her his comic.
Priya came back from the dentist.
She finished her rock drawing.
The bell rang early.
items.hint: Read what Leo did. Then read what Maya and Leo were doing at the end.
items.explain: Maya felt better because Leo made room for her and shared his comic. By the end, they were laughing together.

reason.clue: He slid over to make room.
reason.know: Being invited to join others can end a lonely feeling.
reason.so: So Maya felt better because Leo included her.

items.prompt: Why did Ana spend the morning flipping through channels?
options: She was let down that the final was moved.
She was tired from practice.
She was waiting for her favorite show.
Ben was busy with a video game.
items.hint: Read what Ana was going to do in the final. Then read what Coach Novak said that morning.
items.explain: Ana was let down that the final was moved. She was going to take the corner kick, so she put her cleats away and could not settle on a show.

reason.clue: Ana put her cleats back in the closet without a word.
reason.know: People go quiet and restless when something they worked for is delayed.
reason.so: So Ana felt let down about the final.

items.prompt: Why did Ana shake her head when Ben wanted to play a game?
options: She was still upset about the final.
She did not know how to play.
She was busy with homework.
She wanted to play outside in the rain.
items.hint: Read what happened to the final that morning. Think about how Ana felt about it.
items.explain: Ana was still upset that the final was moved, so even a game did not seem fun.

reason.know: When people feel let down, even fun things can seem dull.
reason.so: So Ana said no because she still felt upset.

items.prompt: Why did Ana jump up after she read the message?
options: She could still practice the corner kick that day.
The final was about to start.
Ben needed help with his game.
The rain had stopped.
items.hint: Read what the message said the team could do that afternoon.
items.explain: Ana jumped up because she could still practice the corner kick in the indoor gym that afternoon.

items.prompt: Why did Leo ride a faster circle after the slow one?
options: He was pleased that the chain he fixed was working.
He was late for school.
Mr. Okafor told him to hurry.
The chain was still loose.
items.hint: Read what happened on the third try. Then think about why someone would test a bike faster.
items.explain: Leo rode faster because the chain he fixed was working. On the third try, it sat straight and the pedals turned smoothly.

reason.know: Testing something you fixed yourself feels good when it works.
reason.so: So Leo rode faster because his fix worked.

items.prompt: Why did Leo leave the gloves on the kitchen table for everyone to see?
options: He was proud that he fixed the chain himself.
He forgot to put them away.
He wanted to give them back.
His mom asked to see them.
items.hint: Read what Leo did that evening before he left the gloves out.
items.explain: Leo was proud that he fixed his chain himself. He told the story twice and left the gloves where everyone could see them.

reason.clue: That evening, Leo told his mom the whole story twice.
reason.know: People retell a story when they are proud of what happened.
reason.so: So Leo was proud he fixed it himself.

items.prompt: Why did Leo ask whether the shop needed an extra helper on Saturdays?
options: Fixing the chain made him want to learn more about bikes.
He needed money for a new bike.
Mr. Okafor asked him to work there.
His mom told him to find a job.
items.hint: Read what Leo had just done before he asked. How might that make him feel about bikes?
items.explain: Fixing his own chain made Leo want to learn more about bikes, so he asked about helping at the shop.

reason.clue: On the third try, the chain sat straight.
reason.know: Success at a new skill can make people want to learn more.
reason.so: So Leo wanted to learn more about fixing bikes.

items.prompt: Why did Priya lean so close to the screen?
options: She wanted to understand how the arm was told what to do.
She could not see without her glasses.
The guide asked her to read the list aloud.
items.hint: Read what the guide said about the arms. Then read what Priya asked to see.
items.explain: Priya wanted to understand how the arm was told what to do. She asked to see the list of moves and leaned in to read it.

reason.clue: Priya asked if she could see the list.
reason.know: Curious people move closer to learn how something works.
reason.so: So Priya leaned in to learn how it worked.

items.prompt: Why did Priya start writing commands on the bus home?
options: The lab gave her an idea for her own rover.
Her teacher gave her homework.
She was bored on the bus.
items.hint: Think about what Priya saw at the lab. Then read what she wrote commands for.
items.explain: The lab gave Priya an idea. She saw how commands tell a robot arm what to do, so she started writing some for her own rover.

reason.clue: She asked three more questions before the guide could finish the tour.
reason.know: When people learn something exciting, they want to try it themselves.
reason.so: So Priya wanted to program her rover the same way.

steps.say: The question asks why Ben grinned. First I find where he grins.
A feeling often comes right after something happens. So I read the sentence just before.
Ana held up a shiny key.
Earlier, Ben's key was gone. So this is the key he was looking for.
Ben grinned because Ana found his key.
